title: Cornell Precollege Studies Summer Residential Program
description: Cornell's Precollege Studies Summer Residential Program lets rising juniors and seniors take real Cornell undergraduate courses alongside Cornell students, choosing from three- or six-week offerings across disciplines including architecture, business, computer science, engineering, hospitality management, international relations, and veterinary medicine. Courses compress roughly 15 weeks of college coursework into the 3- or 6-week session and are taught directly by Cornell faculty rather than a separate pre-college teaching staff. Students live on campus in residence halls under a 1:10 staff-to-student supervision ratio, with Residential Coordinators running structured evening and weekend group activities. The program draws participants from more than 50 countries and nearly every U.S. state, and successfully completed courses appear on an official Cornell transcript.
selectivity_evidence: No published acceptance rate. The application requires a transcript, personal statement, and letters of recommendation; Cornell states admission is based on 'demonstrated academic ability, maturity, and intellectual curiosity' and the overall strength of the application rather than automatic enrollment once eligibility (age 16-18, completed 10th grade) is met.

title: Duke Pre-College Program
description: Duke Pre-College is Duke University's current pre-college summer offering for high schoolers, having succeeded the university's earlier Duke TIP Summer Studies program (which was permanently discontinued in 2020). It runs as a 12-day intensive residential program (a commuter option exists but is limited to middle schoolers) across three summer sessions, with students choosing one course from areas such as entrepreneurship and financial markets, biomedical and mechanical engineering, artificial intelligence, criminal law and advocacy, neuroscience, and creative writing/screenwriting. Each day is split into a morning block (9:00 AM-12:15 PM) and afternoon block (1:30-4:45 PM) mixing lectures, case studies, hands-on labs, and simulations that build toward a capstone assignment. Courses are taught by Duke PhD and graduate students, sometimes alongside guest lecturers from Duke faculty and local industry. It is open to current 9th-12th graders who are at least 14 years old at the session start and have completed one year of high school.
selectivity_evidence: Enrollment is prerequisite-based (minimum age 14, completed one year of high school, 3.0 GPA 'recommended' but not required) rather than competitively reviewed; no essay or recommendation letter is required, and Duke's own program materials describe a rolling enrollment and payment process rather than an admission decision.

title: Johns Hopkins CTY Summer Residential Program
description: Johns Hopkins' Center for Talented Youth (CTY) runs three-week, on-campus summer courses for advanced learners, offered in both day (commuter) and residential (sleepaway) formats at sites across California, Maryland, New York, Pennsylvania, and Rhode Island. Courses span science and engineering, computer science and technology, language arts, mathematics, and history/social studies, taught in small classes that emphasize discussion-based, student-centered instruction over straight lecture. Unlike an open-enrollment camp, students must first establish eligibility through CTY's Talent Search by taking an above-grade-level standardized test (such as the SCAT, SAT, or ACT), and most courses require a minimum qualifying score before a student can register, though CTY notes some select courses do not. Residential students live in campus housing with round-the-clock supervision and take part in organized evening and weekend activities alongside their coursework.
selectivity_evidence: Enrollment requires prior qualification through CTY's Talent Search, in which students take an above-grade-level standardized test (SCAT, SAT, or ACT); many courses require scoring at a specified high percentile to become eligible, a real gating mechanism distinct from simple paid registration, though CTY states a minority of courses waive the minimum score requirement.

title: Northwestern CTD 3-Week Academic Summer Camps
description: Northwestern's Center for Talent Development (CTD) runs 3-Week Academic Summer Camps on its Evanston campus for students entering grades 6-12, with day, 'partnership' day, and full residential options. Students choose one course from two tracks: 'Advanced Enrichment,' interdisciplinary exploration across math, science, writing, and technology, or 'Accelerated' courses that compress one to two semesters of content, including AP and other high-school-credit-bearing classes. Classes run 9:00 AM-3:00 PM on campus with 1-3 hours of nightly homework depending on course type, taught by instructors CTD describes as selected specifically for experience teaching high-ability students in that grade band. Access is gated by an eligibility tier ('Indigo' for accelerated/credit courses, 'Magenta' for enrichment courses) that CTD assigns from a student's test scores, transcript with teacher recommendation, or prior CTD program history, rather than open registration.
application_requirements: eligibility tier verification (test scores/transcript or prior CTD participation)
selectivity_evidence: Enrollment is gated by an eligibility tier system (e.g., 'Indigo' for accelerated/credit courses, 'Magenta' for enrichment courses) that CTD assigns based on standardized test scores, transcripts with teacher recommendations, or prior CTD program participation, rather than open, unscreened registration.

title: Stanford Pre-Collegiate Summer Institutes
description: Stanford Pre-Collegiate Summer Institutes is an entirely online program for students in grades 8-11 (a few courses admit grade 12), delivering one intensive course per two-week session from a catalog of roughly 75 offerings spanning artificial intelligence, biomedical engineering, data science, machine learning, entrepreneurship, finance, philosophy, journalism, creative writing, and environmental studies. Each course meets live for two hours a day, Monday-Friday, for real-time discussion with an instructor plus additional office hours and asynchronous assignments, requiring a computer, webcam, and reliable internet. Courses are ungraded and carry no academic credit; instead of a transcript, students receive written instructor feedback and a Certificate of Completion. Admission requires ranking up to three preferred courses, with Stanford assigning only one course per admitted student, and instructors are described by Stanford as scholars in their fields who are 'passionate about teaching.'
selectivity_evidence: No published acceptance rate. The application requires an unofficial transcript and a ranked list of up to three course choices, with Stanford assigning only one course 'if admitted' -- indicating a real admission decision and capacity constraint rather than guaranteed placement for every applicant.

title: Penn Pre-College Program (Residential)
description: Penn's Pre-College Residential Program places high schoolers directly into credit-bearing University of Pennsylvania undergraduate courses for six weeks over the summer, living in campus residence halls alongside Penn's own undergraduates. Course options include Introduction to Biology and General Physics (with labs), World Film History, English Literature, Philosophy, Medicine in History, Microeconomics, Psychology, and Law and Society, taught by Penn faculty, staff, and visiting scholars rather than a separate pre-college teaching corps. Students typically enroll in one course unit (roughly a four-semester-hour equivalent course), though some add a lab or a second course for up to 2.5 units total. It is open to current 10th and 11th graders, including international students on an F-1 visa (who must enroll in at least 1.5 course units), and there is also a separate non-residential online track for students who cannot attend in person.
selectivity_evidence: No published acceptance rate, but the application requires a minimum 3.5 GPA, three short essays, one letter of recommendation on letterhead referencing the specific program, and a full-year transcript, evaluated through a formal application review rather than open registration.

title: Emory Pre-College Program
description: Emory's Pre-College Program is a noncredit, two-week summer program (residential for about 90% of students, with a commuter option) that gives rising juniors and seniors college-level coursework taught directly by Emory faculty from schools including the College of Arts & Sciences, the Nursing School, and the Rollins School of Public Health. Classes average around 14 students and are graded satisfactory/unsatisfactory rather than by letter grade, with homework that can run up to several hours a day; students choose from 30+ two-week course options across the summer's sessions. Beyond the classroom, the program runs 'College 101' workshops and degree-exploration sessions plus 'Eagle Excursions' to Atlanta attractions such as the Georgia Aquarium and World of Coca-Cola. It is distinct from Emory's separate credit-bearing 'Summer College' program, and is open to students at least 15 years old by orientation who are currently in 10th or 11th grade with a minimum 3.0 GPA.
selectivity_evidence: No published acceptance rate. The application requires a minimum 3.0 GPA, high school transcript, standardized test scores (PSAT/SAT/ACT), and two teacher or counselor recommendations, evaluated on a rolling basis until each session fills.
